newsitem.title: UK: Dollar seen sustaining solid tone in data-packed week.
newsitem.headline: Dollar seen sustaining solid tone in data-packed week.

text.p: The dollar looks set to maintain its firm tone, underpinned by expectations that a slate of U.S. economic data due for release this week will keep interest rate rise speculation on the boil, analysts said on Monday.

A rise of 262,000 in U.S. non-farm payrolls in December, released last Friday, helped fire interest rate rise fever, even more so as an increase in average hourly earnings of 0.5 percent set inflation alarm bells ringing.
Widening U.S.-German yield spreads and its resilience to credit market gyrations buoy the U.S. unit, analysts said.
"Dollar/mark should continue to benefit from the increasing interest rate spread between the U.S. and Germany," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London.

The dollar remained close to 29-month highs against the mark at 1.5870 marks at 1330 GMT, up from 1.5855 at Friday's close. Against the yen it traded at 116.48, up from 115.98 but below its 45-month high at 117 yen hit on January 6.
Norfield said a strong dollar signal was coming from the yield differential between 10-year bonds in real terms.

The 10-year yield spread between the U.S. and Germany has widened to 0.84 percentage points from 0.6 in December, he said. "The widening yield spread gives higher returns against Germany, leaving the dollar with pretty decent support," he said.

The December jobs report led many economists to revise their economic forecasts upwards. Some see a growing risk of a rise in U.S. rates at the next meeting of the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on February 4-5.
December consumer price data, due on Tuesday, will be closely watched for further signs of inflationary pressure.
Analysts polled by Reuters expect an overall CPI reading of 0.3 percent, the same as last month. The core rate, exluding volatile food and energy prices, was expected at 0.2 percent.
December retail sales figures, also due on Tuesday, as well as industrial production figures on Friday, will also be key.
Retail sales are expected to pick up sharply, from a negative 0.4 percent in November to a rise of 0.5 percent. Excluding cars, sales should rise slightly from 0.3 percent to 0.4 percent.

The risk of a dollar setback from U.S. data, in particular if CPI figures were stronger than expected, looked less threatening after the currency's resilient performance after the payrolls' release, traders said.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell nearly two points on Friday to 6.90 percent before recovering back to 6.85 percent. But the dollar shrugged off bond market fears, broke key resistance at 1.5840 marks and set a fresh two-year high.
"The dollar will now head for 1.60. There is stil good demand for dollars, especially as the mark is weak across the board," said Nick Shamin, currency analyst at Technical Data.
Dollar-positive interest rate expectations were highlighted last week by another rise in German unemployment in December and a downbeat outlook for fourth quarter 1996 growth in Germany.

U.S. November trade data, due for release on Friday, could be a thorn in the dollar's side and will be scrutinised for signs of a widening gap with Japan. The overall deficit is seen rising to $9.8 billion from $7.99 billion the previous month.
Even though U.S. rate rise speculation has increased, market watchers caution that the optimism might be premature.
Dollar/yen has been volatile lately amid rumours of Japanese capital repatriation as a result of sharp losses in Japan's stockmarket. However, so far there is little evidence of that.

"We still see an upside bias on dollar/yen," sad ABN Amro's Norfield. "This view is based on capital outflows out of Japan by investors looking for higher yield and the shaky financial prospects of investing in Japan."
Japanese officials dished out plenty of verbal intervention last week to stem the yen's decline.
